name: St Anne’s House (formerly Thornhill) — excavated mansion remains, portico and entrance
address: Former St Anne’s House site, St Anne’s Park, Raheny, Dublin 5, Ireland
historical_period: Early nineteenth century origins; major Guinness-era enlargement from 1835 and remodelling from 1873; fire 1943; demolition 1968
historical_description: Archaeological remains of the former mansion, including in-situ external and internal walls, room surfaces, window recesses, cellar remains, the front portico foundations, front-step and entrance features, porch tile panels, parts of the picture gallery, and the remains of the carriage-road surface. The 2024 community excavation report documents the southern and western portions of the mansion footprint and records a 450 m² excavation area. The house began as Thornhill, was acquired by Arthur and Benjamin Lee Guinness in 1835, expanded over subsequent decades, remodelled from 1873, gutted by fire in December 1943 and demolished in 1968.
historical_significance: The surviving archaeological fabric provides direct physical evidence of the architectural development, domestic interiors, circulation, construction materials and destruction of a major Dublin estate mansion. The excavated encaustic tiles, Portland-stone façade, Dublin calp-limestone portico foundations, jostle stone, heating infrastructure and carriage-road surface supplement historic maps and photographs. The archaeological report also records that the mansion's remains survive beneath demolition deposits and later imported soil.
access_status: The excavation area is an archaeological site and may not be open for unsupervised access. Photograph only from designated public paths or during authorised Dublin City Council community archaeology events. Do not enter fenced areas, excavate, remove objects or disturb the ground.

Record the landscape context and relationship to the historic avenue and Herculanean Temple
Do not photograph or publish sensitive excavation details beyond official public interpretation
coordinate_source: The archaeological report includes a site-location figure and excavation plan but no verified WGS84 point for this specific feature in the reviewed text. No coordinate assigned.
research_notes: Evidence: Dublin City Council's preliminary archaeological excavation report dated 20 November 2024, licence 22E0688 ext. It documents the 2024 excavation of the mansion's portico, porch, picture gallery, part of the main hall and carriage road, plus previous investigations of the drawing room, statue room and cellars. Exact present-day access and exposed condition require field verification.

name: Church of St John the Baptist — seventeenth-century church ruins

historical_description: Roofless remains of a freestanding Church of Ireland church built circa 1610, incorporating earlier fabric. NIAH records a four-bay nave, west entrance porch and bell-cote, north transept, rubble-stone walls, round-headed window openings with limestone or brick detailing, and pointed-arch door openings. name: Clontarf Castle — Gothic Revival country house, rebuilt 1836–37

historical_description: Detached country house rebuilt in 1836–37, comprising a square-plan tower-house form with curved corners and a taller rear tower, attached to a complex-plan Gothic Revival house with gabled bays, porch and canted bay windows. NIAH records carved limestone copings and finials, crenellated parapets, octagonal chimneystacks, carved door surrounds and extensive surviving interior features including plasterwork ceilings, timber wainscoting and joinery, fireplaces and encaustic tiled floors. The NIAH appraisal identifies its carved stonework and surviving interior craftsmanship as significant.

name: 86 Clontarf Road
address: 86 Clontarf Road, Clontarf, Dublin 3
historical_description: Terraced two-bay, two-storey house over a raised basement, built in 1847, with a two-storey return to the rear. NIAH records a pitched M-profile natural slate roof, front parapet with cut-granite platband and cornice, smooth-rendered chimneystacks, Flemish-bond brown-brick front elevation, granite stringcourse and rendered basement. The round-headed entrance has a petal-motif fanlight, a corniced and friezed door surround supported by console brackets, and a timber-panelled door. Cut-granite entrance steps and platform retain a cast-iron balustrade; the property is set back behind cast-iron railings on a cut-granite plinth and a pedestrian gate. A two-bay single-storey outbuilding survives to the rear, with later extensions.
historical_significance: NIAH identifies the house as part of a substantial terrace built in 1847 by Isaac Warren, steward of the Vernon estate, on land obtained from that estate. The terrace, its outbuildings, associated former gate lodge and shared green form a largely intact example of large-scale mid-nineteenth-century housing development along the Clontarf seafront. Historic fabric survives particularly at the entrance platform, door surround and railings.

name: Dublin United Tramway Company Powerhouse (Windmill Lane Recording Studios) — RPS 7381
address: 20 Ringsend Road, Dublin 4, D04 CF66
historical_description: A surviving Art Deco former electrical power station built for the Dublin United Tramways Company. Specialist architectural history identifies Vincent Kelly as architect and dates the building to 1932. The current occupier confirms that No. 20 Ringsend Road was once the electrical power station for the tramline depot and that the recording studios have occupied the building since 1990. Dublin City Council's current Record of Protected Structures lists RPS 7381 as the Ringsend Shelbourne Pierrot Club (former Bovril building), described as a commercial warehouse/sound studio. The sources indicate a layered industrial and cultural history: tramway electricity generation, later Bovril-associated use, and recording-studio use. The exact chronology of the intermediate Bovril phase requires further archival confirmation.
historical_significance: A surviving physical link to Dublin's electric tramway infrastructure and a notable Art Deco industrial building later adapted for music recording. It also illustrates the reuse of former industrial buildings in the Docklands. The current recording-studio use gives the building a continuing cultural role, but private interiors are not part of public access.

name: Poolbeg Lighthouse — red navigation light at the seaward end of the Great South Wall

historical_description: The red lighthouse at the seaward end of the Great South Wall, marking the entrance to Dublin Port. Dublin Port records that the light was first lit on 29 September 1767, replacing a floating light previously used to warn shipping. The Dictionary of Irish Architects records John Smyth's responsibility for the lighthouse's construction in 1766–1767 and the eastern abutment of the South Wall in or after 1771. The exact chronology of later alterations is not fully established by the sources reviewed for this record.
historical_significance: A landmark piece of Dublin's maritime navigation and harbour-engineering infrastructure, physically associated with the Great South Wall and the historic entrance to the port.

name: Former Pigeon House Hotel (Teach Pigeon) — late-Georgian harbour hotel
address: Pigeon House Road, Poolbeg Peninsula, Dublin 4
historical_description: Classical dressed-ashlar granite building of three storeys over basement, with full-height bows at either end of the south-east elevation and entrance facing the Liffey and its harbour. Construction commenced in 1793 and was completed in 1795; design attributed to Robert Pool. Built for cross-channel passengers, it became part of the historic Pigeon House defence precinct in 1798 and remained within the precinct until 1897. The 3FM EIAR records it as standing. The Film Office lists short-term office/location use; March 2026 reporting describes rooms used by a wastewater operator under a council letting proposal, whose final terms are not established here.
historical_significance: Rare surviving late-eighteenth-century harbour hotel associated with passenger travel and the later Pigeon House precinct.

name: Sluice House, South Wall — former Rathmines and Pembroke drainage control building (DCIHR 19-09-009-01)
address: Great South Wall, Poolbeg Peninsula, Dublin 4
historical_description: Detached three-bay, single-storey masonry former sluice house built around 1881 in association with Londonbridge Road Pumping Station and the Rathmines and Pembroke Main Drainage Scheme. The 3FM EIAR describes squared-random rubble stone walls with concrete coping and rusticated quoins; segmental-headed window openings with rusticated block-and-start surrounds, now blocked; and a square-headed doorway with rusticated granite surround and a steel door installed around 1990. The building housed machinery operating two penstock valves to manage sewage flow and seawater pressure at the sewer outlet. It is now described as abandoned, retaining much of its original form and stonework.
historical_significance: A surviving example of late-nineteenth-century municipal drainage engineering, associated with Ireland's first completed main sewerage scheme.

name: Magazine Fort — eighteenth-century military powder magazine
address: St Thomas Hill, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8
historical_period: 1734–1736; modified c.1760 and 1801; conservation and phased reopening 2023–2026
historical_description: Freestanding, broadly square-plan military magazine fort with four demi-bastions, watch-towers, an eastern extension and ranges of barrack and magazine buildings. The National Inventory of Architectural Heritage dates the complex to 1730–1810 and describes its principal construction phases around 1735, c.1760 and 1801. It was designed as a powder magazine for Dublin and retains original magazine chambers and evidence of successive military uses. The Office of Public Works led a major conservation programme; the fort reopened for guided public tours in 2026.
historical_significance: A nationally rated military complex associated with the defence and supply infrastructure of Dublin and the 1916 Rising. Its conservation and 2026 reopening make it an especially important current heritage site.

name: Ashtown Castle — restored fortified tower house
address: Phoenix Park Visitor Centre, Chesterfield Avenue, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8
historical_period: c.1605; later incorporated into Ashtown Lodge c.1760; restored in the 1990s
historical_description: Detached three-storey fortified tower house with a square-plan stair tower to the south-east, built around 1605. The building has uncoursed limestone rubble walls, a pitched slate saddle-back roof behind parapets, a dressed-stone chimney, small square-headed windows and defensive loops. It was incorporated into a larger Georgian residence around 1760; that later lodge was subsequently demolished. The tower was restored and now forms part of the Phoenix Park Visitor Centre heritage experience.
historical_significance: A rare surviving fortified house of the early seventeenth century close to Dublin city, preserving evidence of the earlier Ashtown demesne and later park administration.

historical_description: Principal entrance gateway at the city end of Chesterfield Avenue, comprising two pairs of round-plan ashlar limestone vehicular piers with moulded plinths and cornices, gadrooned caps and electrified wrought-metal and glass lanterns. The gate piers were dismantled in 1932 to facilitate the Eucharistic Congress and re-erected in 1986.

historical_description: Detached quadripartite single-storey iron-and-masonry former warehouse over a vaulted basement, built around 1820 to designs by John Rennie. The NIAH records four glazed gables facing south onto Custom House Quay, multiple-bay brick side elevations fronting George's Dock, four natural-slate roofs with continuous lanterns and extensive cast-iron structure. The ironwork was supplied by the Butterley Foundry. The building was extensively renovated and converted for commercial use in 2005 and is now known as the CHQ Building.
historical_significance: A nationally significant late-Georgian industrial building and an exceptional survivor of Dublin's tobacco and bonded-warehouse history, with an unusually large iron-and-masonry interior and vaulted basement.

name: The Design Tower — former Bewley, Moss & Co. sugar refinery
address: Grand Canal Quay, Dublin 2
historical_description: Eight-storey former warehouse built in 1862 for Bewley, Moss & Co. as a sugar refinery, designed by Alfred Derbyshire with engineering advice from Sir William Fairbairn. The NIAH describes rusticated limestone elevations, granite quoins and plinth, dressed granite stringcourses, polychrome brick eaves cornice, cast-iron cresting to the stair tower, pattress plates and round- and segmental-headed openings. It was enlarged in 1890 for use as a distillery. In 1978 the IDA acquired and restored it as an enterprise centre.
historical_significance: A distinctive and technically ambitious industrial building associated with sugar refining and distilling at Grand Canal Dock. Its restoration received a Europa Nostra award in 1983, and the building remains a prominent landmark in the docklands.

name: Pumphouse No. 1 — Alexandra Basin Heritage Zone
address: Alexandra Road, Dublin Port, Dublin 1
historical_period: c.1910; southern section added shortly afterwards
historical_description: Detached gable-ended brick pumphouse built around 1910 beside the southeast corner of the former Graving Dock. historical_significance: A surviving component of Dublin's nineteenth- and twentieth-century ship-repair infrastructure and an important remnant of the former graving-dock precinct. name: Redbrick Electricity Substation — East Wall Road / Alexandra Road
address: Corner of East Wall Road and Alexandra Road, Dublin 1
historical_description: Detached corner-sited two-storey electricity substation built around 1900. The NIAH describes a single-bay breakfronted west elevation and three-bay north elevation, flat roof concealed behind a brick parapet with moulded granite coping, red brick in Flemish bond, moulded brick string course and cornice, gauged round-headed window openings, granite sills and an arched entrance framed by brick Doric piers. Dublin Port states that the building played a pivotal role in the early electrification of the Port. It has been restored and adapted as a museum, with a new largely glazed extension.
historical_significance: A surviving piece of early electrical infrastructure associated with the modernisation of Dublin Port. Its carefully detailed brickwork gives an otherwise utilitarian service building architectural significance. Refurbishment also exposed part of the earlier 1728 sea wall beneath the building; that buried wall is a separate archaeological feature and is not treated as visible fabric of the substation.

name: Dublin Tropical Fruit Company warehouse — Tropical Fruit Warehouse
address: 30–32 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, Dublin 2
historical_period: c.1890; established as Tropical Fruit Company warehouse in 1892; restored and redeveloped 2019–2022
historical_description: Attached double-gable-fronted fourteen-bay two-storey former warehouse built c.1890 for the Dublin Tropical Fruit Company, with its use for tropical-fruit imports recorded from 1892. The NIAH describes an M-profile pitched slate roof set perpendicular to the street with clerestory, terracotta ridge tiles, red-brick Dutch gables with decorative terracotta apex tiles, carved limestone cornice, brick pilasters, limestone string courses, coping and orb finials, Flemish-bond brickwork, polychrome and cogged brick string courses, segmental-headed openings and carved limestone keystones. The historic warehouse was later restored and integrated with a substantial modern office redevelopment, including elevated glazed office floors and a new building to the rear. The historic warehouse fabric must be distinguished from these later additions.
historical_significance: A prominent surviving late-Victorian docklands warehouse and a rare physical record of Dublin's tropical-fruit import trade. Its façade also preserves two earlier riverine keystones associated with Carlisle Bridge and sculptor Edward Smyth. The building's layered history includes the Hibernian Marine School site, the Tropical Fruit Company, later U2 management offices and contemporary adaptive reuse; these phases are documented by different sources and should not be conflated.

name: British & Irish Steam Packet Company offices — The Shipping Office protected structure
address: 20–24 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, at the junction with Lime Street, Dublin 2
historical_period: Built 1909; formally opened 1910; integrated into The Shipping Office redevelopment completed 2025
historical_description: Freestanding six-bay, two-storey former shipping-company offices with attic storey, built in 1909, with integral carriage arches to the end bays, shallow projections to the north frontage, a west wing wall and a triple-pile goods shed to the rear. NIAH records pitched slate roofs with terracotta ridge cresting, red-brick chimneystacks, a red-brick parapet with carved masonry capping, clerestories to the rear store roofs, Flemish-bond brickwork, carved limestone details, round-headed ground-floor windows, oculi, elliptical-headed carriage arches with terracotta keystones, cast-iron wheel stops, a loading platform and cobbled yard. The company moved its offices here in 1909 and the building was formally opened in 1910. The historic structure has since been integrated into the modern mixed-use development known as The Shipping Office; the modern glazed atrium and new office development are later additions and must not be mistaken for the 1909 building.
historical_significance: A surviving protected shipping-office building associated with the British & Irish Steam Packet Company, a major Irish Sea shipping operator established in Dublin in 1836. The building records the commercial and operational history of the port through its offices, carriage arches, rear goods sheds and loading infrastructure. Its classically influenced brick-and-stone façade was designed by W.H. Byrne & Sons. The historic structure now forms part of a contemporary redevelopment, illustrating adaptive reuse of a docklands industrial-era building.

name: The Ferryman — former pair of Georgian houses, 35–36 Sir John Rogerson's Quay
address: 35–36 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, at Cardiff Lane, Dublin 2
historical_description: Corner-sited attached former pair of three-bay, four-storey houses, built c.1820 and now used as a public house and guest house. The National Inventory of Architectural Heritage records an M-profile hipped slate roof, red-brick chimneystacks, red-brick parapet with granite coping, Flemish-bond brick walls, square- and round-headed window openings, granite sills, surviving timber sliding-sash windows, and round-headed door openings with carved Portland-stone architrave and marigold lintel carvings. The two houses were originally separate. NIAH records Michael Scanlon and James Lynch as occupants in the 1850s; contemporary trade directories listed a grocer and shipbuilder at No. 35 and a ship smith at No. 36.
historical_significance: A rare surviving early nineteenth-century quay-side pair that preserves the scale, materials and commercial character of the historic Sir John Rogerson's Quay streetscape. Its carved stone doorcase, timber sash windows and diminishing fenestration are notable architectural details. The site also records the former mix of domestic, retail and maritime trades along the quay.

name: Catholic Seamen's Institute — former Georgian house at 4 Sir John Rogerson's Quay
address: 4 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, Dublin 2
historical_description: Terraced two-bay, four-storey former house built c.1825. The National Inventory of Architectural Heritage records its later use as a charitable hostel and as the Catholic Seamen's Institute, founded by the Society of Saint Vincent de Paul. The recorded fabric includes a hipped corrugated-iron roof behind a brick parapet with granite coping, rendered chimneystacks, brown Flemish-bond brick walls, rendered quoins and platbands, and square-headed window openings with raised rendered reveals and masonry sills. NIAH records visible lettering on the first- and second-floor platbands and vestiges of the institute's sign on the fascia.
historical_significance: The building preserves evidence of the late-Georgian merchant-house group on Sir John Rogerson's Quay and its later adaptation for charitable support of seafarers. The documented sign remnants are a particularly valuable target for recording the building's social history.
access_status: NIAH records the former institute as disused. Current occupancy and public access are not confirmed. Photograph only from a lawful public viewpoint; do not enter the property.

name: Columbia Mills — former H.M. Leask & Company mill, 14–15 Sir John Rogerson's Quay
address: 14–15 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, Dublin 2
historical_description: Attached gable-fronted five-bay, three-storey former mill built c.1890, now recorded by NIAH as offices. The inventory describes a pitched corrugated-steel roof with roof lights behind a parapet with central pediment and painted masonry coping, lined-and-ruled rendered walls, segmental-headed window openings with rendered surrounds and painted masonry sills, and later replacement windows and ground-floor shutters. NIAH records Thomas Crosby's sailcloth and canvas manufacturers on the site in 1880 and H.M. Leask & Company in 1894; the building is associated with Leask's linseed-crushing trade.
historical_significance: Columbia Mills preserves a rare industrial trace within the former mixed-use quay landscape. Its association with sailcloth manufacture and H.M. Leask & Company connects the building to maritime supply trades and to the industrial streetscape described in James Joyce's Ulysses.

name: St Anne’s Park — Roman Tower
address: Hilltop west of the pond, St Anne’s Park, Raheny, Dublin 5
historical_description: Freestanding square-plan three-stage tower with chamfered corners and a granite domed roof. Its cut-sandstone walls are articulated by platbands and stringcourses, with a carved granite plinth. Each elevation of the upper stage has a pedimented Ionic temple-front and round-headed opening. The NIAH records that it originally stood on the roof of St Anne’s House and was moved to its present hilltop location in 1873.
historical_significance: A prominent estate folly and former viewing tower over Dublin Bay. Its classical design was apparently based on the Tomb of the Julii at Saint-Rémy in France; this is the NIAH’s stated design comparison, not a proven direct copy.

name: St Anne’s Park — Annie Lee Tower and Bridge
address: Former entrance avenue to St Anne’s House, St Anne’s Park, Raheny, Dublin 5
historical_description: A pointed-segmental-arch pedestrian bridge with a two-stage octagonal-plan tower at its south-west end. The NIAH describes squared and rubble limestone walls, squared voussoirs, a stringcourse at the arch impost and rebuilt parapets. The tower contains pointed-arch openings, lancet windows, internal steps and chambers. An inscribed plaque was inserted into the east elevation in 1926.
historical_significance: Built by Benjamin Lee Guinness to mark the birth of his first child, Annie Lee. The bridge carried the former entrance avenue over the route to St Anne’s House; the tower and bridge combine a functional crossing with a Gothic Revival-inspired estate folly.

address: Entrance to the walled garden, St Anne’s Park, Raheny, Dublin 5
historical_description: An attached square-plan four-stage bell tower forming the entrance to the walled garden. The NIAH describes yellow-brick walls, a carved granite cornice and stepped parapet with corner finials, a carved shield, a recessed panel with stone cherubs, and an inset clock with a carved surround. The integral round-headed arch has a carved limestone keystone and wrought-iron gate. The upper stage contains round-headed openings with carved stone Y-tracery and louvred vents.

It was originally inscribed with Benjamin Lee Guinness’s name and the family motto “Spes Mea in Deo”, as recorded by the NIAH.

name: St Anne’s Park — Herculanean Temple
address: Beside the Naniken River landscape, St Anne’s Park, Raheny, Dublin 5
historical_description: Detached temple folly comprising a semi-circular six-column Ionic portico adjoining a single-bay room to the south. The NIAH describes a flat concrete roof, cut-limestone architrave and frieze with remains of carved wreaths and swags, carved Ionic columns on a granite plinth wall, and wrought-iron railings between the columns. name: St Anne’s Park — remains of the earlier walled garden
address: Eastern side of the former St Anne’s House site, St Anne’s Park, Raheny, Dublin 5
historical_description: Surviving remains of an earlier estate walled garden, built c.1820 before the Guinness family acquired Thornhill in 1835. name: St Anne’s Park — double-arch bridge incorporating a hermitage
address: Naniken River and adjoining footpath, St Anne’s Park, Raheny, Dublin 5
historical_description: A double-arch bridge carrying a road over the Naniken River and a pedestrian path, incorporating a small hermitage. The NIAH describes rubble-limestone spandrels and parapets with cobble coping, roughly squared limestone stringcourses, pointed arches over the river and southern footpath, and pointed-arch openings to the hermitage. The NIAH notes that it replaced an earlier timber bridge shown on the first-edition Ordnance Survey map, and that the hermitage reflects the nineteenth-century fashion for simulated rustic retreats.

name: Anna Liffey riverine keystone — salvaged Carlisle Bridge carving
address: Set into the street-facing façade of the Tropical Fruit Warehouse, 30–32 Sir John Rogerson's Quay, Dublin 2; west-side riverine keystone
historical_period: Sculpted 1794; originally associated with Carlisle Bridge; later incorporated into the Tropical Fruit Company warehouse façade, relocation date not established
historical_description: One of two original riverine figurehead keystones incorporated into the façade of the former Tropical Fruit Company warehouse. NIAH identifies the west-side head as Anna Liffey and states that the riverine keystones were sculpted by Edward Smyth in 1794 for Carlisle Bridge. When Carlisle Bridge was reconstructed as O'Connell Bridge in 1880, the original keystones were too large for the altered arches; smaller replicas were made, and the originals later found their way to the warehouse façade. The precise date and circumstances of their relocation are not established by the sources consulted.
historical_significance: An individually significant surviving piece of eighteenth-century Dublin sculpture, retaining an original carved river-god keystone from the predecessor of O'Connell Bridge. It connects the history of the Liffey crossing, the work of sculptor Edward Smyth and the later maritime warehouse on Sir John Rogerson's Quay.

historical_description: The 3FM Great South Wall heritage report states that the 1759 Ballast Office Wall consisted of two parallel rubble walls with a sand-filled space between them. Although much of this stretch now lies beneath Pigeon House Road, some sections of its boundary walls remain visible as low parapet walls. The report does not provide individual parapet segment coordinates, lengths, exact locations or a current-condition guarantee.
historical_significance: These low parapet remnants are rare above-ground traces of the earlier Ballast Office Wall, distinct from the later Great South Wall extension towards Poolbeg. They preserve the visible edge of an eighteenth-century harbour-engineering work whose main alignment is now largely concealed beneath the road.

name: Huband Bridge — 1791 Grand Canal bridge and parapet lamp standard
address: Huband Bridge, connecting Mount Street Crescent with Percy Place, Dublin 2
historical_description: Single-arch humpbacked bridge spanning the Grand Canal, built in 1791. The bridge has an ashlar granite arch and parapet walls over dressed limestone piers, with cast-iron balustrades between panelled limestone piers. A central limestone plaque bears the name Huband Bridge and the date 1791; a cast-iron lamp standard stands over the north parapet coping. A canal lock lies nearby.
historical_significance: An unusually complete historic canal crossing whose bridge masonry, inscribed plaque, cast-iron balustrades and parapet lamp standard form a coherent heritage ensemble. NIAH associates the bridge with Joseph Huband, a director of the Grand Canal Company, and notes its continued use.

name: Wood Quay — surviving Hiberno-Norse city wall section

historical_description: A surviving section of Dublin's first Hiberno-Norse stone city wall, dated to approximately 1100. name: Boland's warehouse/mill at lifting bridge — six-storey stone warehouse
address: 1 Ringsend Road, Dublin 4
historical_period: 19th century; exact construction date not established in the sources consulted
historical_description: A surviving six-storey stone warehouse forming part of the historic Boland's Mills complex at Grand Canal Dock. Dublin City Council's Record of Protected Structures identifies the building as the Boland's warehouse/mill at the lifting bridge on Ringsend Road (RPS 7377). Conservation architects BKD describe the existing six-storey stone quayside building as a mill later converted to a silo; it was conserved and retrofitted as part of the completed Bolands Quay development. The wider industrial complex included other buildings and structures, some of which were removed or redeveloped; this record is specifically for the surviving stone warehouse building, not the entire former complex.
historical_significance: A surviving piece of Dublin's grain-milling and docklands industrial history, retaining historic stone industrial fabric within the modern Grand Canal Dock setting. The former Boland's Mills site is also associated with the industrial and commercial development of the docklands; this individual building is recorded as a protected structure (RPS 7377).

name: Kilmainham Mill — former flour and textile mill complex
address: Kilmainham Lane / Rowserstown Lane, Kilmainham, Dublin 8
historical_period: c.1815–1825; expanded in the mid-to-late 19th century
historical_description: A surviving early nineteenth-century industrial mill complex beside the River Camac. The National Inventory of Architectural Heritage records an attached L-plan, four-storey former flour mill built c.1820, with a two-storey brick extension and later concrete extension. Dublin City Council's September 2023 project briefing records a mid-to-late nineteenth-century expansion that included a steam engine, a rerouted headrace serving a new water wheel, a cast-iron sectional aqueduct and cast-iron internal columns. The mill later changed from flour and corn processing to cloth finishing around 1903/04; industrial activity ceased in 2000. This record covers the surviving mill complex, not the medieval predecessor mill: the earlier water-powered activity is evidenced historically but is not catalogued here as a separately located surviving structure.
historical_significance: A rare surviving example of Dublin's early nineteenth-century milling and textile-finishing industry, retaining evidence of successive power and production systems beside the River Camac. Dublin City Council described it in 2023 as the last remaining largely unaltered early nineteenth-century flour mill in Dublin and probably the last remaining fulling mill in Ireland.
access_status: The complex is owned by Dublin City Council. DCC's September 2023 briefing states that accessibility was limited and facilities for widespread use were not available at that time. Do not enter the site, buildings or work areas without explicit permission. Confirm current public access and photography permission with Dublin City Council before any visit; photograph only from lawful public viewpoints.

name: Former Pigeon House Lifeboat House — archaeological site with surviving wall stubs (DCIHR 19-09-008)
address: Great South Wall, near Poolbeg Lighthouse, Dublin 4
historical_period: c.1850; lifeboat presence at Pigeon House recorded as early as 1815
historical_description: The 3FM EIAR catalogue identifies the Lifeboat House as a site, not a complete standing building. It records a lifeboat at Pigeon House as early as 1815, although it was apparently later transferred to Bullock. For the c.1850 lifeboat-house site, only lengths of ruined wall stubs remain above ground; surviving fabric includes red brick and granite. An enclosure wall of old concrete construction also survives, breached in places, and the perimeter path is ruinous from coastal processes. A historical photograph from 1939 in Dublin Port Archives shows standing remains at the station site.

name: Masonry landing slip at eastern entrance to Pigeon House Fort (DCIHR 19-09-012)
address: Great South Wall beside the eastern entrance to Pigeon House Fort, Dublin 4
historical_description: A substantial masonry boat slip adjoining the Great South Wall beside the eastern entrance to Pigeon House Fort. The 3FM EIAR catalogue records it as constructed around 1770 and shown on both the Ordnance Survey First Edition 6-inch series and 25-inch maps. It measures approximately 25m long and 4.3m wide, slopes gently west-to-east at about 10 degrees, and has a surface of rectangular granite masonry similar to the facing blocks of the adjacent Great South Wall. The report records it standing up to 1.6m above the foreshore, with four courses of granite masonry visible; sheet piles protrude from silty sand on the channel side.

name: Scherzer rolling-lift bridges over the North Wall lock
address: North Wall Quay at the lock near Guild Street, Dublin 1
historical_description: Pair of single-span bascule or rolling-lift bridges installed over the lock in 1911–1912. The NIAH identifies the Scherzer rolling-lift mechanism, supplied by Spencer and Company of Melksham to designs by Sir John Purser Griffith, based on the system patented by William Scherzer. The bridges replaced an earlier Turner and Gibson drawbridge installed in 1860 and are carried on battered granite ashlar retaining walls.
historical_significance: An important surviving example of early-twentieth-century movable-bridge engineering and a distinctive part of the North Wall's railway and dock infrastructure.

name: George's Dock — Georgian wet dock and lock entrances
address: Custom House Quay, Dublin 1
historical_description: Rectangular stone wet dock built in 1821 to designs by engineer John Rennie. The NIAH records squared coursed limestone ashlar walls, slightly battered and capped with large squared granite coping, with curved walls at both lock entrances, granite bollards and cast-iron mooring ties around the perimeter. The dock connects northwards to the Inner Dock and southwards to the River Liffey. Its modern use includes public events, with a later steel deck structure and contemporary water and railing features.
historical_significance: A major piece of Georgian harbour engineering associated with John Rennie and the development of Dublin's port; its stone walls, lock geometry and mooring fittings preserve the form of the original wet dock.

name: Custom House Quay — Georgian granite ashlar quay

historical_description: Granite ashlar quay built around 1790 as part of the continuous sequence of quays defining the north side of the River Liffey. name: Loop Line Railway Viaduct — Beresford Place and Liffey crossing
address: Beresford Place, Gardiner Street Lower and River Liffey, Dublin 1
historical_description: Thirteen-span railway viaduct built around 1891 to carry the City of Dublin Junction Railway across Beresford Place and the River Liffey, connecting Connolly Station with the line to Dún Laoghaire. The NIAH describes four stylistically distinct components: a three-span steel girder bridge over Gardiner Street Lower with riveted decorative parapet panels and cylindrical columns; a two-span masonry arch section with yellow-brick voussoirs and rusticated limestone spandrels; a five-span steel girder section over Beresford Place with lattice parapets and granite piers; and a three-span Liffey crossing with fish-belly girders supported on cast-iron caissons. The Beresford Place piers include Portland-stone classical detailing.
historical_significance: A major work of late-Victorian railway engineering by John Challoner Smith, built by Arroll Brothers of Glasgow. It connected the Dublin and Wicklow railway route with Amiens Street (Connolly) Station and supported the Royal Mail route. Its combination of steel, masonry, granite, Portland stone and cast-iron caissons makes it an unusually rich subject for architectural and engineering documentation.

name: Sheriff Street Lifting Bridge — Spencer Dock bascule bridge
address: Sheriff Street Upper over Spencer Dock, Dublin 1
historical_description: Single-span bascule bridge installed over Spencer Dock between 1939 and 1941. The NIAH records that it is now fixed and retains a pair of reclaimed cut-limestone panels with rope-twist detailing and the date “1873”, carrying the emblem of the Midland Great Western Railway of Ireland. These panels recall the earlier Spencer Swivel Bridge designed by James Price and opened in 1873, the first mechanical crossing over Spencer Dock. The 1941 bridge was reported to have cost £18,000 and was described at the time as a structure unique of its kind in Ireland.
historical_significance: An important surviving docklands engineering structure that combines a twentieth-century bascule bridge with reused nineteenth-century railway heraldic panels, preserving evidence of two successive mechanical crossings at Spencer Dock.

name: George's Dock Lock — limestone lock to the River Liffey
address: South side of George's Dock, between the dock basin and River Liffey, Dublin 1
historical_description: Limestone lock built around 1820 connecting George's Dock to the River Liffey. name: Grand Canal Docks — historic L-plan basin
address: Grand Canal Dock, Hanover Quay / Grand Canal Quay / South Dock Road, Dublin 2
historical_description: L-plan canal basin built in 1796 as the docks for the Grand Canal, designed by engineer William Jessop. The NIAH records roughly coursed calp-limestone walls with squared calp and tooled-granite coping, cast-iron bollards and mooring posts, dressed-granite and later rendered steps, three sea locks at the north-east and dry docks at the east end. A modern road bridge carrying Pearse Street replaced an earlier drawbridge.
historical_significance: A major late-eighteenth-century civil-engineering and maritime site, designed to connect ocean-going shipping with the Grand Canal's inland network. The NIAH describes it as a twenty-five-acre basin designed for 150 ocean-going vessels and, at opening, the largest canal dock in the British Isles.

name: Westmoreland, Buckingham and Camden Sea Locks — Grand Canal Dock entrance
address: North-east entrance of Grand Canal Dock at the River Liffey, Dublin 2
historical_description: Group of three sea locks built in 1796 to connect Grand Canal Dock with the tidal River Liffey. The NIAH records tooled-granite walls and coping on the central dock platforms, inscriptions recording names and dates, machinery notches and lock-gate emplacements, cast-iron ladders and rings, three sets of double-leaf timber gates with timber beams and some later metal panels, stone setts and limestone paving, and winch mechanisms on the eastern and central platforms. The locks were named Westmoreland, Buckingham and Camden after English viceroys. Westmoreland was intended for canal boats; Camden and Buckingham for ocean-going vessels.
historical_significance: The sea locks were essential to managing the tidal difference between the River Liffey and the still-water canal basin. They are a rare, highly legible ensemble of late-eighteenth-century maritime engineering. Waterways Ireland announced a Camden Lock restoration initiative in 2026; the current state and operational status of each gate must be checked on site and not inferred from older NIAH descriptions.

name: McKenny Bridge — former Conyngham Bridge
address: Junction of Mount Street Lower and Northumberland Road, Dublin 2
historical_description: Single-arch granite canal bridge built around 1790 to carry the road over the Grand Canal. The NIAH records coursed-granite parapets, stringcourses and copings, projecting piers, a segmental arch with voussoirs and hood-moulding on the east elevation, and flat concrete lintelling with a rebuilt parapet on the widened west side. A carved limestone plaque on the east elevation reads “McKenny Bridge”; a memorial commemorating the 1916 Battle of Mount Street stands to the south-west. The bridge was originally named Conyngham Bridge and later renamed for Thomas McKenny, chairman of the Grand Canal Company.
historical_significance: An important surviving structure from the first decades of the Grand Canal, showing later widening and a layered naming history. Its carved bridge-name plaque and nearby 1916 memorial are separate details to document carefully.

name: Dublin Port Diving Bell — Stoney's compressed-air quay-construction caisson
address: Sir John Rogerson's Quay, Dublin 2
historical_period: Designed mid-nineteenth century; delivered 1866; entered service 1871; fabricated c.1870; used until 1958
historical_description: Cast-iron and riveted plate-iron diving bell designed by Dublin Port engineer Bindon Blood Stoney and built by Grendon and Company of Drogheda. The NIAH describes a chamber approximately 23 feet square by 6.5 feet high, accessed by a vertical shaft with iron rungs and incorporating an air lock. The bell was lowered from a floating platform so workers could excavate and level the riverbed under compressed air before large precast concrete quay-wall blocks were placed. It was moved to Sir John Rogerson's Quay in 1989 and is mounted on a modern display structure.
historical_significance: An exceptionally important surviving artefact of nineteenth-century harbour engineering and compressed-air construction. Dublin Port's archive records its role in building the North Wall Extension and Alexandra Basin; the bell is now part of Dublin Port's Distributed Museum and a publicly accessible interpretive installation.

name: Great South Wall — registered historic sea wall and breakwater
address: Linear maritime monument extending from the Dodder estuary / Ringsend towards Poolbeg Lighthouse, Dublin Bay; not represented by a single point coordinate
historical_period: 1715–1795, with multiple construction phases and later alterations
historical_description: The Great South Wall is a long, phased maritime engineering structure associated with the development of Dublin Port. The 3FM heritage report describes the piled works initiated in the early eighteenth century, the Ballast Office Wall completed in 1759, and the later masonry extension towards Poolbeg and the lighthouse. The Great South Wall is identified in the report as a registered archaeological monument and protected structure. Its component sections differ in construction and present visibility; parts are buried, missing above ground, or remain visible as wall and parapet sections.
historical_significance: A major eighteenth-century engineering work that shaped the navigation channel and Dublin's relationship with Dublin Bay. Its surviving and buried sections preserve evidence of harbour engineering, coastal protection, port development and successive construction methods.
national_inventory_reference: RMP DU018-066 and DU019-029; Dublin City Council RPS 6928 (as cited in the 3FM report)
access_status: The wall is a long linear monument crossing public, port-owned, industrial and restricted areas. Public access varies by segment and may change. Do not assume the full route or every surviving wall section is accessible.
photography_restrictions: Do not enter port or ESB lands, industrial sites, fenced compounds, the cooling-water outfall or restricted areas. Photograph only from lawful public viewpoints and obey all barriers, signs and site rules. Never climb the wall or approach exposed water edges in unsafe conditions.

Do not conflate the Ballast Office Wall (1759) with the later granite-faced Great South Wall extension towards Poolbeg.

historical_description: The Board of Ordnance constructed a gun battery on the Great South Wall in 1793, approximately 800m from Poolbeg Lighthouse, to control the river channel and waters around the lighthouse. The 3FM EIAR catalogue describes it as armed with five 24-pounder guns, subsequently dismantled, with part of the structure surviving. The south-facing perimeter wall is granite-built and is the most intact upstanding element; a curvature in the Great South Wall surface is believed to mark a former gun swivel position. The present site includes the Half Moon swimming-place and club buildings. A separate Dublin Port Heritage Conservation Strategy describes the battery as a three-gun platform, so the historical gun-count requires source reconciliation.
historical_significance: Surviving coastal-defence fabric associated with the late-eighteenth-century protection of Dublin Bay and the approach to the Liffey.
access_status: The site is associated with an active swimming club and Great South Wall. Do not enter club buildings or restricted areas without permission; photograph only from lawful public access and respect swimmers and club operations.

name: Wellington Monument (Wellington Testimonial)
address: South-eastern Phoenix Park, near Islandbridge Gate, Dublin 8
historical_description: Freestanding granite obelisk, 62 metres tall, designed by Sir Robert Smirke as a testimonial to Arthur Wellesley, Duke of Wellington. The monument stands on a three-stepped monumental pedestal and a square-plan stylobate. Four bronze plaques cast from cannons captured at Waterloo are set into its faces; three carry bas-reliefs and the eastern face bears a Latin and English inscription. The monument is also known as the Wellington Testimonial.
historical_significance: A nationally rated monumental work and one of the defining nineteenth-century features of Phoenix Park. Its bronze plaques, relief sculpture and inscriptions make it a multi-part visual and epigraphic subject.
access_status: Located in Phoenix Park. Photograph from public paths and safe viewpoints; respect any temporary barriers, events or maintenance closures. Do not cross fences or approach unsafe slopes.

name: The Phoenix Monument — Portland-stone Corinthian column and phoenix
address: Central roundabout, Chesterfield Avenue, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8
historical_description: Freestanding Portland-stone Corinthian column erected in 1747 and surmounted by a carved stone phoenix rising from the ashes. The full-height fluted shaft has a Corinthian capital and stands on a plinth with inscribed marble plaques to the east and west and carved coats of arms to the north and south. Its stepped granite base is enclosed within a circular platform of stone setts. The monument stands at the central junction of Chesterfield Avenue, Acres Road and Odd Lamp Road.
historical_significance: One of the earliest surviving features of Phoenix Park and a focal point on its principal avenue. The column, phoenix sculpture, plaques, heraldry and surrounding stone-sett platform each merit separate visual documentation.
access_status: The monument occupies the centre of a road junction/roundabout. Do not enter the carriageway or traffic island. Photograph only from safe public paths and viewpoints.

name: Papal Cross — 1979 papal mass steel monument
address: Fifteen Acres, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8
historical_description: Freestanding steel cross erected in 1979 on a granite-flagged platform atop a grass-covered mound approached by a flight of thirty-three granite-flagged steps. Designed by Ronnie Tallon of Scott Tallon Walker for the outdoor Papal Mass celebrated by Pope John Paul II during his first and only pastoral visit to Ireland. The National Inventory describes the cross as 35 metres high and weighing 31 tonnes, formed from steel I-beams produced by J. & C. McGloughlin, Inchicore, and requiring approximately five kilometres of welding. A commemorative plaque records the Mass of 29 September 1979 and the congregation of more than one million people.
historical_significance: A nationally rated monument and major work of late twentieth-century engineering, associated with one of the largest public gatherings in modern Irish history.
access_status: Located in the public park. Photograph from the public path and platform where permitted; respect temporary event barriers and avoid climbing the cross or surrounding structures.

name: Knockmaree burial monument — surviving Neolithic cist
address: Knockmaree / Knockmary, west of St Mary's Hospital, Phoenix Park, Dublin 8
historical_period: Late Neolithic burial mound with later Early Bronze Age burials; excavated in the nineteenth century
historical_description: A Linkardstown-type burial monument recorded as National Monument Service record DU018-00711. The Phoenix Park Conservation Management Plan describes a cemetery mound originally about 40 metres wide and up to 3 metres high. Excavation revealed a central cist formed by five upright stones supporting a large capstone; the cist is the only element of the original mound recorded as surviving. The central burial included at least three male inhumations and grave goods including a shell necklace, bone toggle and flint blade. Four small Early Bronze Age cists containing cremated remains and food vessels were also recorded. The exact age and sequence should be expressed using the archaeological report's period terms rather than an unsupported single calendar date.
historical_significance: A rare surviving prehistoric funerary structure within Phoenix Park, documenting Neolithic and Early Bronze Age burial practices and the long archaeological history of the park landscape.
access_status: Within Phoenix Park near St Mary's Hospital. Use public paths and follow park notices. Do not climb on, touch, clean, move objects around or disturb the cist; report any damage or dumped material to the park authority.

name: St Anne’s Well — medieval holy well and nineteenth-century stone surround
address: St Anne’s Park, Raheny, Dublin 5, Ireland
historical_description: A holy well recorded by Dublin City Council as medieval and listed on the Record of Monuments and Places as DU019-012. The visible well structure and surrounding works were also modified in the nineteenth century by the Guinness family. Archaeological monitoring in 2016 recorded the original circular opening at the base, with a nineteenth-century metal grille still in place, and a granite-paved section extending 2.45 metres from the well opening. The well had been dry for decades at the time of the 2016 report; an account from 1902 described it as a fine spring of water.
historical_significance: The well gave St Anne’s Park its name and is a documented archaeological and devotional feature within the estate landscape. It is important to distinguish the well's medieval attribution and protected-monument status from the visible stone surround and metal grille, which include nineteenth-century fabric. The archaeological monitoring report found no archaeological material during the cleaning works; this does not negate the site's recorded monument status.
access_status: Photograph only from designated public paths and where access is clearly permitted. Do not enter, touch, clear vegetation, remove material or interfere with the well or its grille; it is a protected recorded monument.

name: Glasnevin Cemetery — O'Connell Circle and its sunken vault street
address: Glasnevin Cemetery, Finglas Road, Dublin 11, Ireland
historical_description: Multiple-bay circular vault and landscaped cemetery feature built c.1840. A circular street of family vaults is accessed by a sunken channel; the surface is laid out with funerary monuments in concentric circles. Vault entrances have brick jambs, granite lintels inscribed with family names, four-panel cast-iron doors and fixed numbers. Stone bridges cross the channel to the central section, with granite steps and flagged floors.
historical_significance: An original and nationally rated cemetery landscape designed by Patrick Byrne, conceived as the showpiece of the New Ground and formerly the temporary burial place of Daniel O'Connell before his reinterment beneath the round tower in 1869.

name: George's Dock Arch — relocated limestone triumphal arch

name: St Anne’s Park — shell house with ‘The House that Jack built’ pier

name: James’s Street — Francis Sandys 1790 drinking fountain and sundial obelisk

name: Inner Dock
address: George's Dock, Dublin 1, County Dublin, Ireland
historical_description: Rectangular stone wet dock, built 1824, to designs of John Rennie with lock opening into Georges Dock to south. Developed c.1997 as residential development with five apartment blocks built along north and east perimeters and further two blocks built on concrete piles to centre of dock. Built of squared coursed limestone ashlar walls, slightly battered with large squared granite coping, replaced with concrete to southeast end. Curved walls to all corners with iron ladders to southeast and northwest corners. Several cast-iron mooring ties and rings located to south and west perimeter. Enclosed to south and west by iron bollards and chain-fence with concrete and iron footbridge connecting south wall to apartment complex.
historical_significance: This stone-built dock was designed by John Rennie who also designed the Tobacco Warehouse (50010003) and several dock structures in London. Named after George IV, who travelled to Ireland in 1821 to officially open the dock, he failed to turn up and was instead opened by Lord Castlecoote. Standing as testament to the exemplary stone masonry skills of the early nineteenth-century, the retention of the dock has provided a tranquil waterside setting for what was the first residential docklands development in the Irish Financial Services Centre.

name: The Oasis Centre
address: Saint Laurence Place East, Emerald Street, Dublin 1, County Dublin, Ireland
historical_description: Detached multiple-bay two-storey red brick and limestone convent, built 1882, to designs of John Loftus Robinson. Now in use as drugs counselling and support centre. Symmetrical front elevation with central gabled entrance projection, three-sided two-storey projections to either end and seven-bay two-storey projection to rear. Two-bay two-storey addition to south, c.1915. Hipped artificial slate roofs with terracotta ridge tiles, pyramidal to canted projections with Celtic cross iron finials. Several decorative brick and limestone chimneystacks and moulded cast-iron guttering on moulded red brick eaves course and cast-iron downpipes. Red brick walls laid in English bond with chamfered rock-faced limestone plinth course and flush limestone ashlar lintel and sill courses. Square-headed window openings with chamfered surrounds, moulded limestone shoulder stones to first floor, splayed limestone sills and replacement uPVC windows with red and black brick relieving arches over ground floor windows. North canted projection contains convent chapel of c.1905 with pointed-arch window openings having red and black brick relieving arches, splayed sills on continuous limestone sill course, stained-glass windows and weather glazing. Decorative advanced gabled entrance bay with limestone coping and Celtic cross finial having Gothic niche with canopy and limestone statue of Saint Laurence on cherub-headed corbel and flanked by lancets. Weathered limestone below first floor sill level with pointed-arch door opening and polychromatic brick relieving arch and hood-moulding with compound moulded brick head to deeply inset door with splayed brick reveals and pair of inset limestone bootscraper niches with iron brackets. Diagonally-sheeted double-leaf timber doors with iron door furniture and stone over-panel with quatrefoil light. Door opens onto granite platform and three granite steps to front garden enclosed to street by decorative iron railings on low red brick wall with limestone plinth and coping having matching iron gates on decorative brick and limestone piers with decorative limestone capstones. Tarmac to rear site used for parking. Interior to single-cell chapel having exposed roof with braced timber trusses on corbels, plaster walls, leaded stained-glass windows to east elevation with simple marble altar furniture and choir balcony to west.
historical_significance: This is a very fine red brick and limestone convent building displaying attractive stone carving and ornamentation. Founded by the Sisters of Charity in 1882 the convent was supported by donations from a rising Catholic middle class whose generous support permitted such a splendid example of ecclesiastical architecture. The convent is entirely characteristic of the 1880s and exhibits the influence of the Gothic Revival movement in its rich detailing. Composed of very high quality materials the building has survived in excellent condition and is still in use as a convent, and also as a counselling centre, continuing to contribute to the community of which it has long been an important part.

name: Connolly Station
address: Amiens Street, Dublin 1, County Dublin, Ireland
historical_description: Freestanding brick and limestone water tower with iron tank, built c.1880, with adjacent wrought-iron and timber turntable. Comprising three stone walls with brown brick facing, east and central walls have full-height brick arch with rock-faced limestone ashlar walls. Surmounted by granite coping supporting full length riveted iron tank carried on iron I-beams. Now faced to southwest by timber sheeted billboard. Wrought-iron turntable immediately to southwest having iron tracks over timber sleepers, cast-iron turntable. Cut limestone chamber on round plan with red brick coping at ground level. Located in close proximity to railway platform at Connolly Station.
historical_significance: This simple water tower with well-executed arches, is an example of good quality design being used for utilitarian railway structures. The brick and stonework are of a high standard and the contrasting materials contribute to the visual appeal of the structure. The survival of the tower and the adjacent turntable, in good condition, contributes greatly to the historic heritage of Connolly Station and its surroundings and is testament to the high quality craftsmanship during the great age of the Victorian railways.

name: Saint Agatha's Church Presbytery
address: 46 William Street North, Dublin 1, County Dublin, Ireland
historical_description: Detached three-bay two-storey presbytery, built c.1900, having projecting pedimented porch to centre of front (south) elevation. Hipped artificial slate roof with rendered chimneystacks and clay ridge tiles. Cast-iron gutters to overhanging corbelled eaves, with cast-iron downpipes. Pitched artificial slate roof to porch. Ruled-and-lined render walls with rendered plinth and rendered platband to first floor sill level. Engaged Doric corner pilasters to rendered porch supporting closed bed pediment. Square-headed window openings with moulded rendered surrounds and sills throughout, having six-over-six pane timber sliding sash windows to house and four-over-four pane windows to porch. Square-headed door opening to porch with uPVC door and single concrete step. Located within own grounds, set back from street bounded by recent steel railings. Recent garage to rear of site.
historical_significance: This finely appointed building was constructed to provide housing for priests ministering at the adjacent Saint Agatha's Catholic Church. The church took thirty years to complete and occupies a challenging, constricted site behind Charleville Mall, which dates from the 1830s. The North Strand area was bombed in 1941 and the nearby buildings were damaged at that time. Much new local authority housing was constructed in the locality after the bombing. This presbytery retains most of its original form and character and continues to play a vital role in the religious life of the local community.

name: Saint Vincent's Boys' National School
address: William Street North, Dunne Street, Dublin 1, County Dublin, Ireland
historical_description: Detached corner-sited five-bay three-storey school over raised basement, built 1904. Single-bay three-storey block to rear elevation with exposed basement level. Flat roofs with overhanging eaves and cast-iron rainwater goods. Recessed rendered panels to wall having separating bands and quoin bands of red brick in Flemish bond. Red brick platband over basement level to front elevation and having chamfered granite plinth course throughout. Square-headed window openings throughout having patent rendered reveals and replacement multiple-pane windows. Square-headed window openings to basement level having wrought-iron window bars, red brick reveals and concrete lintels. Pointed-arch door opening to front (south) elevation, having gauged red brick voussoirs, chamfered reveals and timber-framed overlight and sidelights over timber recessed panels. Timber panelled double-leaf doors having herringbone pattern, brass door handles and kick plate having single granite step to street level. Street-fronted with recent flat-roofed school buildings to rear of site.
historical_significance: This school is an interesting transitional building which demonstrates elements of the Modern Movement with its flat roof, large rendered panels at the side and rear elevations, while retaining much of the red brick embellishments more characteristic of the turn of the twentieth century. The pointed-arch door and moulded brick lend an almost nostalgic tone to the front elevation of this tall, even imposing building, in a narrow street. Saint Vincent's Boys' School, which is located adjacent to Saint Agatha's Church, has played a vital role in the educational and social life of the area for more than a century. It is also of cultural significance as the former school of writer Brendan Behan. The school was set up by the Daughters of Charity who follow the teachings of Saint Vincent de Paul and Saint Louise de Marillac. They celebrated 150 years in North William Street in 2007.

name: Charleville Mall Library
address: 16-17 Charleville Mall, Dunne Street, Dublin 1, County Dublin, Ireland
historical_description: Corner-sited attached multiple-bay single-storey red brick library, built 1899, to designs of C.J. McCarthy, on loose T-plan. Three-bay gabled breakfront to west of principal/front (north) elevation. Former Carnegie community hall, built 1910, attached to east. Pitched replacement corrugated-iron roofs throughout, with corbelled eaves course and cast-iron rainwater goods. Red brick parapet walls to gables having dentillated red brick architraves and tooled stone architraves, having red brick kneelers with dentillated decoration. English garden wall bond red brick walls with chamfered brick plinth course and moulded brick string courses to springing level of window arches continuing as hood-mouldings. Terracotta plaque with shaped apron to advanced gable reads 'Public Library'. Segmental-arched window openings with gauged red brick voussoirs, moulded brick hood-mouldings and stone sills over recessed aprons, paired to north elevation and in tripartite arrangement at advanced gable. One-over-one pane timber sliding sash windows throughout, with recent steel shutter boxes over. Round-headed door opening within moulded brick surround having chamfered reveals, keystone and blind fanlight. Double-leaf timber panelled doors giving access to interior porch having terracotta tiled floor. Accessed via limestone platform with cast-iron bootscraper, limestone steps and recent cobble lock ramp with steel handrails. Round-headed door opening to side (west) elevation within moulded brick surround with chamfered reveals, keystone and replacement double-leaf timber panelled doors giving access to adjoining community hall. Interior recently renovated.
historical_significance: Designed by Charles J. McCarthy, this picturesque red brick public library, with delightful moulded brick embellishments, abounds in detail and charm. The extension, which housed the separate children's, ladies' and reference rooms was funded by the philanthropist Andrew Carnegie. The building exhibits the influence of the Arts and Crafts movement of the late nineteenth century in the asymmetrical layout of the front elevation, the use of hood-mouldings and the prominent gables. The library forms an appealing architectural landmark in the streetscape, adjacent to Saint Agatha's Church and the terrace of houses on Charleville Mall.

name: Eagle Motors
address: 46-49 North Great Clarence Street, Dunne Street, Dublin, County Dublin, Ireland
historical_description: Attached corner-sited L-plan complex of industrial buildings, built c.1900, comprising two dressed rubble limestone buildings with corner-sited red brick former foreman's house to southwest corner. Complex now in use as commercial premises. Triple-gabled three-bay two-storey elevation with attic storey facing south onto North Great Clarence Street having two carriage arches. Pitched corrugated fibre cement roofs with red brick eaves course, cast-iron rainwater goods, partially replaced. No visible chimneystack. Snecked rubble limestone walls with red brick dressings forming platbands and string courses. Corrugated-iron section to second floor level of east elevation. Oculus window openings to each gable having red brick surrounds, window to west having iron grille, central window with fixed single-pane window, easternmost window partially removed. Camber-headed window openings to ground and first floors, having moulded red brick block-and-start surrounds, granite sills and keystones. Fixed multiple-pane windows behind wrought-iron grilles. Camber-headed window opening to ground floor, now blocked. Camber-headed carriage opening having red brick block-and-start surround, gauged red brick voussoirs and granite keystone. Recent steel door with pedestrian wicket and cast-iron carriage stops. Recent square-headed carriage entrance having steel lintel and recent brick surround to steel gate. Square-headed loading bay to first floor, having red brick and limestone surround with recent concrete lintel and sill. Five-bay two-storey block facing west on to Dunne Street. Hipped artificial slate roof with red brick chimneystacks, stepped red brick eaves course and cast-iron rainwater goods. Snecked rubble limestone walls with red brick dressings forming platbands and string courses, with squared limestone quoins to corners. Camber-headed window openings with moulded red brick block-and-start surrounds, gauged red brick voussoirs, granite sills and keystones. Fixed multiple-pane windows behind wrought-iron grilles to first floor. Ground floor openings now blocked. Camber-headed carriage opening having red brick block-and-start surrounds, gauged voussoirs, granite keystone and cast-iron carriage stops. Recent sliding steel door to interior on rail. Two-bay two-storey red brick house to southwest corner of complex, having pitched artificial slate roof, red brick chimneystack shared with adjoining warehouse to north and cast-iron rainwater goods. Timber bargeboards to gables and eaves. English garden wall bond red brick walls with chamfered brick plinth course. Roughcast render and timber studs rising from bressamer to west-facing gable. Camber-headed window openings with red brick reveals, granite sills and multiple-pane timber casement windows. Square-headed window openings to side (south) elevation, having gauged red brick voussoirs, granite sills and timber casement windows. Square-headed door opening with red brick reveals and replacement timber door. Side elevation continued by single-storey extension to east holding square-headed door opening giving access to rear yard.
historical_significance: This substantial warehouse complex, which has survived largely intact, forms a pleasant landmark within the streetscape. The red brick foreman's house, which occupies one corner of the complex, adds a degree of diversity in both materials and treatment, clearly articulating a hierarchy of uses. This house is an attractive domestic building whose red brick construction contrasts with the robust dressed limestone of the two warehouse buildings. The severe limestone elevations are greatly enlivened by red brick dressings and, in particular, by the block-and-start surrounds and oculus windows. The cast-iron carriage stops are unusual features and testify to the nature of the carts which served the warehouses in their heyday.

name: Meehan Associates
address: 81 Amiens Street, Dublin 1, County Dublin, Ireland
historical_description: Terraced three-bay two-storey house over raised basement, built c.1832, now in use as offices. Part of terrace of seven similarly-scaled buildings. Recent extension to north abuts single-storey recent buildings. Late nineteenth-century limestone ruin to rear. Flat roof concealed behind yellow brick parapet wall with squared granite coping. Two stepped yellow brick chimneystacks with clay pots to party wall, shared with No.82 to south. Replacement aluminium rainwater goods to rear. Flemish bond yellow brick walls with rendered granite plinth course over rendered basement to front (east) and rear elevations. Cast-iron lanterns flanking central doorcase, and recent brass and timber sign to front elevation. Side (north) elevation wall on diagonal, narrowing to two-bay elevation at rear, with recent single-bay and three-bay extensions to side (north) elevation. Square-headed window openings with gauged brick voussoirs, rendered reveals and granite sills with replacement uPVC windows throughout. Central three-centred-arch door opening with gauged brick voussoirs, moulded surround and painted timber and stone doorcase. Replacement timber panelled door flanked by engaged Ionic columns on plinth blocks, with lintel cornice forming support to single-pane replacement fanlight. Victorian doorbell to reveal. Door opens onto granite-flagged platform with cast-iron bootscraper and granite-stepped approach bridging basement area. Approach flanked by wrought-iron railings with cast-iron finials to corners on partial replacement granite plinth having matching gate giving access to basement via recent steel staircase. Detached three-bay two-storey coursed random rubble ruin to rear of site, partially cement rendered, with no roof and south and east walls largely intact. Truncated gauged brick flat-arched window openings with red and yellow brick block-and-start surrounds and granite sills. Red brick relieving arches over timber lintels to interior blind window openings. Blind entry to south infilled with masonry and render. Matching boundary wall on axis with south wall attaching to rear elevation of building.
historical_significance: Amiens Street was laid out from the early eighteenth century and formed the north-eastern boundary of the Gardiner Estate c.1800, although it developed largely in the early nineteenth century in connection with the canal and railway. This building forms part of modest terrace which offers variation from the ubiquitous, grand Georgian townhouse. It is the only three-bay structure on the terrace with the addition of an unusual central entry which, along with Nos.82 and 87, was among the first to be built. A relic of its siting at the corner of Amiens Street and Seville Place is the diagonal north wall which narrows the structure to two bays at the rear. Although heavily altered, the building maintains an original doorcase as well as railings and assists in bolstering the formal Georgian streetscape by virtue of its shared parapet line and overall massing. It also retains an unusual late nineteenth-century ruin to the rear. Timber lintels, relieving arches and truncated window openings, hearken to an earlier period and add texture to the streetscape.

name: Liffey Oil Ltd
address: 84 Amiens Street, Dublin 1, County Dublin, Ireland
historical_description: Terraced two-bay two-storey house over raised basement, built c.1832, now in use as office. Part of terrace of seven similarly-scaled buildings. Shared recent extension to rear (east). M-profile hipped slate roof with hips to north behind yellow brick parapet wall with squared granite coping. Two stepped partially-rendered yellow brick chimneystacks with clay pots to party wall, shared with No.85 to south. Aluminium rainwater goods to rear. Flemish bond yellow brick walls with rendered granite plinth course over rendered walls to basement. Rear (east) elevation of yellow brick in English garden wall bond with granite plinth course over cement-rendered basement. Recent brass sign flanking doorcase reading: 'Liffey Oil Ltd' and possible circuit box casing reading 'Oxford' to north of doorcase. Square-headed window openings with gauged brick voussoirs, rendered reveals and granite sills, having replacement uPVC windows throughout. Recent cast-iron window guards to basement opening and steel window guards to rear elevation openings. Three-centred-arch door opening with gauged brick voussoirs, moulded surround and painted timber and stone doorcase. Replacement timber panelled door flanked by engaged Ionic columns on plinth blocks, with lintel cornice forming support to single-pane replacement fanlight. Door opens onto granite flagged platform shared with No.83, having cast-iron bootscraper and granite stepped approach bridging basement area. Approach flanked by wrought-iron railings with cast-iron corner finials on granite plinth. Projecting wall to west of basement area having artificial slate roof and original timber door with cast-iron door furniture. Original cast-iron coal hole cover set in granite slab to front pavement. Rear of site flanked by steel fence and matching gate on low rubble stone wall.
historical_significance: This modest former townhouse forms an integral component of an intact terrace of informally paired buildings whose massing offers variety from the ubiquitous three and four-storey Georgian streetscape. Despite the loss of some original features, the building retains an original doorcase, vault access door and its original fenestration pattern, and shares a common parapet line and overall composition with its neighbours. It importantly assists in bolstering the original Georgian character of the street. Situated at the former northeast boundary of the Gardiner Estate, Amiens Street was laid out from the early eighteenth century and was renamed after Viscount Amiens, the first Earl of Aldborough, before developing further in the nineteenth century in conjunction with the canals and railway.

name: Fulcrum Office Suites
address: 85 Amiens Street, Dublin 1, County Dublin, Ireland
historical_description: Terraced two-bay two-storey house over raised basement, built c.1832, now in use as offices. Part of terrace of seven similarly-scaled buildings. Square-headed window openings with gauged brick voussoirs, rendered reveals and granite sills with replacement uPVC windows throughout. Steel window guards to rear elevation window openings. Three-centred-arch door opening with gauged brick voussoirs, moulded surround and painted timber and stone doorcase. Replacement timber panelled door flanked by engaged Ionic columns on rendered plinth blocks incorporating bases, with lintel cornices forming support to single-pane replacement fanlight. Door opens onto shared granite flagged platform with remnants of cast-iron bootscraper and granite stepped approach bridging limestone flagged basement area. Approach flanked by wrought-iron railings with cast-iron corner finials on replacement granite plinths. Rendered basement dividing wall with clay ridge tiles. historical_significance: This pleasant former townhouse is an important component of a largely intact early to mid-nineteenth-century terrace whose transitional Regency design recalls the outward development of the city, connecting the Georgian centre and Victorian outskirts. The building contributes to the uniformity of the terrace, sharing similar massing, fenestration arrangements and parapet heights which augment the formal Georgian streetscape, now largely muddled in this developed thoroughfare. Although altered, the building has retained a pleasant doorcase, railings, coal hole cover and an appropriate slate roof. Formerly known as The Strand, Amiens Street was laid out in the early eighteenth century and developed largely in the nineteenth, forming the northeast boundary of the Gardiner Estate c.1800.

name: Health Service Executive — house (NIAH 50010114)
address: 109 Amiens Street, Dublin 1, County Dublin, Ireland
historical_description: Terraced three-bay three-storey house over raised basement, built c.1810. Built as one of pair with shared integral carriage opening. Now in use as offices. Hipped slate roof behind parapet with granite coping, no visible chimneystack. Cast-iron hopper and downpipe. Red brick walling laid down in Flemish bond. Granite plinth course over rendered wall to basement area. Gauged red brick flat-arched window openings, with patent rendered reveals, painted sills, and replacement uPVC windows. Square-headed window opening to basement area with replacement uPVC window. Round-headed door opening with stone surround and replacement timber panelled door flanked by engaged Ionic columns supporting fluted frieze and stepped cornice with replacement leaded fanlight. Approached via concrete platform with three granite steps, flanked by wrought-iron handrails. Elliptical-headed opening to carriage arch with gauged red brick voussoirs, timber panel to arch head. Recent steel double-leaf gates give access to rear. Area bounded by granite plinths surmounted by original wrought-iron railings with spike finials. Corner posts with remains of pine cone finials.
historical_significance: This house stands on Amiens Street, originally known as 'The Strand', its name changed c.1800 in honour of Viscount Amiens, later the Earl of Aldborough. This group of houses was built in the style characteristic of the early Georgian period with pleasing portions and fine detailing. The character of the surrounding area was greatly impacted by the arrival of the railway within a couple of decades of the construction of the houses. The survival of the Adamesque doorcase contributes greatly to its architectural heritage significance. The front elevation is further enhanced by the elegant shared carriage opening to the centre of the pair of houses which contributes to the texture and variety of the streetscape.
